claim: Sampling/averaging search (UCT) cannot tell shallow forced-loss moves (trap level 5-7) from good moves; shallow traps occur in about 7-15% of mid-game chess positions (about 12% in grandmaster games at 47 ply) but are rare in Go.
agent_test: Plant a one-move fatal-refutation item in our task set; check if sampled-and-averaged scoring accepts it vs an exhaustive code check, at equal tokens.

claim: More rollouts do not fix trap blindness: with 10x the minimax node count, UCT trap value stays above -0.15 at levels 5 and 7, and wasted depth grows exponentially with trap depth.
agent_test: Raise samples 4x on trap items; if accuracy stays flat, route to exhaustive check.

claim: MCTS is more susceptible to shallow traps than alpha-beta (Baier and Winands 2018; Ramanujan et al.). Evaluation-guided informed rollouts (MCTS-IR-E, no minimax) beat random-rollout MCTS-Solver at 96.8% in Catch the Lion, 79.9% in Othello and 75.4% in Breakthrough, so playout value matters; whether shallow-minimax hybrids specifically repair trap blindness is shown by the paper's separate hybrid experiments, not by these figures.
agent_test: Add a shallow exhaustive verifier pass to sampled chains; compare vs sampling only.
audit_note: The 96.8 / 79.9 / 75.4% win rates are real but belong to MCTS-IR-E, informed rollouts guided by a static state evaluation (no minimax), against random-rollout MCTS-Solver; the paper itself says adding shallow searches into rollouts did not improve MCTS-IR, so these numbers do not show that a shallow minimax hybrid repairs trap blindness or that trap density drives the gain (hybrid vs alpha-beta win rates are 66.9% Breakthrough, 17.4% Catch the Lion, 26.9% Othello).
claim_before_audit: Trap blindness is partly separable from weak playout value: giving MCTS a shallow minimax (hybrid) repairs it, most where traps are dense (informed rollouts vs random-rollout MCTS-Solver: Catch the Lion 96.8%, Othello 79.9%, Breakthrough 75.4% win rate).

claim: Plain alpha-beta still beats the best MCTS-minimax hybrid in 2 of 3 games (hybrid wins 66.9% Breakthrough, 17.4% Catch the Lion, 26.9% Othello): MCTS is not a universal upgrade over exhaustive search.
agent_test: Compare tree search vs exhaustive-checker baseline on a tactical subset.

claim: UCT can be provably over-optimistic: worst-case early regret is a tower of exponentials in depth; for D=20 the transition phase is about 10^156837 trials. Asymptotic convergence says nothing about small budgets.
agent_test: Test by depth sweep on deceptive-reward puzzles (worst case itself is a construction).
audit_note: Three evidence lines are the same Coquelin and Munos paper (arXiv cs/0703062 and its 2014 re-upload 1408.2028, UAI 2007) and the fourth is a Wikipedia page with no numbers. Content check: the paper does give a double-exponential bound with 10^156837 at D=20 for the square-root confidence sequence and a D-1 composed-exponential bound for the usual log sequence, so the 10^156837 figure belongs to the sqrt variant, not standard UCT.

claim: A learned policy/value network lets MCTS beat Stockfish (AlphaZero), so evaluator quality matters a great deal for chess-like games; Baier and Winands note deep RL evaluators seem to avoid traps well, yet MCTS stays more trap-susceptible than alpha-beta whatever the evaluator, so the weakness is reduced, not shown to be removed.
agent_test: Replace a prompted LLM judge value with a code-checked value where possible; compare.
audit_note: Silver et al. show AlphaZero defeating Stockfish, but Baier and Winands (2018) say that regardless of the state evaluator MCTS remains more susceptible to traps than alpha-beta; the conclusion that the limit is value-model quality rather than the search loop is an inference, and the Feng et al. line (Game24 15.5 vs 19.1) is about LLM decoding, not chess.
claim_before_audit: A learned policy/value network largely removes the chess weakness (AlphaZero beat Stockfish), so the limit is value-model quality rather than the search loop.

claim: Superhuman MCTS agents keep systematic evaluator blind spots: a cyclic adversary beats KataGo 95.7% (1007/1052) at 4096 visits and 72% (50 games) at 10^7 visits; search lowers but does not remove the exploit.
agent_test: Run held-out adversarial items against our evaluator; check whether more search budget closes the gap.

claim: Patching one exploit does not close the class: three defences failed against freshly trained adversaries (90% with 26% of defence compute; 81% with 5%; 42% even at 65,536 visits for one victim).
agent_test: Hold out failure families when checking a fix; do not count patched cases as closure.

claim: Frontier-lab report: MCTS with a fine-grained value for token-level reasoning did not scale (DeepSeek-R1 appendix); search helps at inference only with a pre-trained value model. Counterpoint: rStar-Math (d08) succeeds with MCTS and a step value trained from code-verified outcomes, so the failure is specific to unlearned or fine-grained token-level values.
agent_test: Prefer few sampled attempts plus code-checked selection over deep trees.

claim: At equal generation budget, standard MCTS with an LLM does not beat repeated sampling on ARC-AGI (Pass@2 sampling 15.0/18.6 vs MCTS 9.0/14.0 for GPT-4o/DeepSeek-V3 at 128 generations) and is mixed on code (average rank over 6 settings: sampling 3.5, MCTS 4.2; MCTS wins on DeepSeek-V3 code).
agent_test: Equal-token comparison of sampling vs tree on our ARC subset.
audit_note: Wu et al. (MATH, REBASE vs MCTS vs sampling) is a different task family and only supports the general direction; the ARC and code numbers all come from Inoue et al. (AB-MCTS), whose table matches exactly.

claim: Tree-search gains depend on adaptive width and an external signal: adaptive-branching MCTS beats repeated sampling on CodeContest from budget 32 and on three MLE-Bench tasks (GPT-4o, n=1), while on ARC sampling only plateaus near 512 generations.
agent_test: Test adaptive vs fixed width at equal tokens.

claim: Standard MCTS spends dozens of times more tokens than sampling or voting because rollouts rarely reach final answers; a rollout-free reward-balanced tree (REBASE) beats both on MATH500 (Mistral-7B 45.0% at 1.36e14 FLOPs vs sampling 42.8% at 8.70e14).
agent_test: Always count rollout tokens in the budget when comparing search to sampling.

claim: Search against an imperfect scorer over-optimizes: beam search hurts on easy MATH levels 1-2, helps on levels 3-4, and no method progresses on level 5; lookahead search underperforms at equal budget.
agent_test: Gate search on estimated difficulty; compare gated vs always-on.

claim: Resampling against an imperfect verifier has a ceiling set by its false-positive rate; the best number of attempts is often under 10 (HumanEval+, MBPP+).
agent_test: Measure the false-positive rate of our checker; cap attempts accordingly.
audit_note: Stroebl et al. give the false-positive ceiling and optimal K often under 10 (K about 5 in Figure 4); Brown et al. support only the general plateau/false-positive point.

claim: Monte Carlo step-value labels are noisy (right answers can come from wrong steps), and PRMs trained on them did significantly worse than ones trained on LLM-as-judge or human labels (Qwen team). Prompted self-exploration with small models is also weak: after 32 RAP rounds only 24% of LLaMA2-7B trajectories on GSM8K are correct, and rStar reports small models have difficulty telling which steps or final answers are correct.
agent_test: Use an independent checker instead of the same model grading its own steps.
audit_note: Qwen team confirm MC-estimation PRMs are significantly worse than LLM-as-judge and human-label PRMs, but in rStar the 24% is the share of RAP trajectories (LLaMA2-7B, GSM8K, 32 rounds) that are correct, a measure of generation quality, not the share judged correct by prompted self-evaluation; rStar separately says small models struggle to tell which steps or answers are right, without that number.
claim_before_audit: Monte Carlo step-value labels are noisy (right answers from wrong steps), PRMs trained on them are worse than ones trained on LLM-judge or human labels, and prompted self-evaluation is unreliable (only 24% of RAP LLaMA2-7B GSM8K trajectories judged correct).

claim: LLM tree planners degrade steeply with plan length: MCTS success under tight budget 1.00, 0.92, 0.50, 0.11, 0.05, 0.00 for L=2..12; RAP Blocksworld LLaMA-33B 1.00/0.88/0.42 for 2/4/6 steps at 20 iterations; extra expansions do not reliably yield optimal plans.
agent_test: Depth sweep on a planning task; test a depth cap plus verification.
audit_note: Zhang et al. say extra search compute 'does not reliably improve' / 'does not necessarily yield' optimal plans, not that it never does; the sources are otherwise exact (tight MCTS row, RAP(20) 1.00/0.88/0.42).
claim_before_audit: LLM tree planners degrade steeply with plan length: MCTS success under tight budget 1.00, 0.92, 0.50, 0.11, 0.05, 0.00 for L=2..12; RAP Blocksworld LLaMA-33B 1.00/0.88/0.42 for 2/4/6 steps at 20 iterations; extra expansions do not give optimal plans.

claim: Budget failure modes differ by algorithm: under tight budgets ToT-BFS 98% search exhaustion, DFS 92%, MCTS 52% exhaustion and 48% budget violation, bidirectional search 92% budget violation.
agent_test: Track budget violations per search operator.

claim: Search helps when a real environment or test signal exists: LATS HumanEval 92.7% (GPT-4), web-agent best-first search +39.7% relative on VWA and +28.0% on WA, ToT Game of 24 74% vs CoT 4%.
agent_test: Enable tree search only where code or test feedback exists.

claim: In sparse-reward deterministic puzzles MCTS-like sampling reverts to near-uniform search; a policy-guided enumeration with an expansion bound (LevinTS) solves 1000/1000 Sokoban levels vs LubyTS(512,32) 884 +/- 4 and uniform 88.
agent_test: Compare bounded best-first enumeration vs sampled search on a puzzle set.

claim: UCT exploration constant matters: in Mancala c=2.5 was best, c=20 gave a minimax-like tree and small c an unfocused tree with weak play; the bound-based fix (BAST) requires smoothness coefficients to be known or assumed.
agent_test: Sweep the exploration constant per task; check the variance of the best value.
audit_note: Mancala c=2.5 and unfocused small-c tree are confirmed (single domain), but 'no safe default' and 'smoothness constants unknown for language' are not stated by Ramanujan-Selman or Coquelin-Munos (BAST just needs smoothness coefficients known/assumed); b06 and c03 are the same paper.
claim_before_audit: Exploration parameters matter and have no safe default: UCT constant c=2.5 was best in Mancala, small c gave an unfocused tree; bound-based fixes need smoothness constants unknown for language.

claim: LLM-evaluator pruning is irreversible and its errors systematic; a calibrated gap threshold gave +4.38 utility points (ToolTree), but the confidence interval excludes zero only at budgets B100 and B200.
agent_test: Do not prune low-scored branches without a held-out calibrated margin.

claim: Sequential backtracking search beats parallel sampling on Sudoku but loses on CountDown at a fixed token budget: the best search style depends on task structure.
agent_test: Equal-token task-by-task comparison of backtracking vs parallel.

claim: Sampling accuracy saturates at a fixed limit set by the model's own output probabilities (Wu et al.); non-reasoning models hit a 'reasoning floor' that more inference compute does not lift, and among reasoning models, verifier-free simple majority voting beats sequential revision and mixture-of-agents (Wang et al.).
agent_test: Hard items should switch operator (reframe, tool), not add depth.
audit_note: Wang et al. show majority voting beating revision and mixture-of-agents only for reasoning models; for non-reasoning models (Llama-3.3-70B) external search occasionally surpasses majority voting, so the unqualified wording is too wide.
claim_before_audit: Sampling accuracy saturates at the model's own probability of correctness; non-reasoning models hit a floor, and without a verifier majority voting beats revision and mixture-of-agents.

claim: With a good PRM, MCTS beats beam search, best-of-N and voting as budget grows (code PRM study), contradicting the 'sampling wins' results; the outcome depends on verifier quality.
agent_test: Run the same item set under a good and a poor checker.

claim: A scored step-level evaluator misses the earliest error on hard problems: on ProcessBench most open PRMs trail prompted general models, and even o1-preview misses 20-30% of wrong responses; no direct LLM test of a single fatal-refutation item exists.
agent_test: Build 20 one-fatal-step items; compare our judge with a code check.

claim: In Stechly et al.'s GPT-4 tests, an LLM self-critique loop lowered accuracy on Game of 24 (5% to 3%) and Graph Coloring (16% to 2%) but not Blocksworld (40% to 55%), while a sound external verifier raised Game of 24 to 36-38% and plain k=25 sampling reached 42%; LLM self-verification can help when scaled over many samples (Zhao et al.).
agent_test: Replace LLM self-critique by a code-run check wherever one exists.
audit_note: Game of 24 numbers match Stechly et al. (5%, 3%, 36-38%, 42%), but LLM critique raised Blocksworld accuracy (40% to 55%), the 'shallow exhaustive code check vs LLM check' sentence is not in either source, and Zhao et al. show LLM self-verification at scale (Verification@200) beating majority voting and o1-Preview.
claim_before_audit: Self-judging verification loops lower accuracy while sound external checks raise it: GPT-4 Game of 24 5% to 3% with LLM critique, 36-38% with a sound verifier, 42% with plain k=25 sampling. A shallow exhaustive code check recovers the gain; an LLM check does not.

claim: Search against a learned evaluator has exploitable blind spots: optimized 100-token suffixes lift PRM reward above 0.9 on flawed reasoning, 43% of an RL reward gain is stylistic, and judge false positives reach up to 35% (punctuation, GPT-4o) and 60-90% ('Thought process:', open 70B+ models) under master keys; a judge trained with adversarial negatives (Master-RM) reached near-0% on the tested attacks.
agent_test: Run a held-out adversarial audit of our own evaluator before enabling pruning.
audit_note: The 100-token PRM suffix (>0.9), 43% style share and 35-90% judge false positives are confirmed, but 'patching one family fixed that family only' is not supported: Zhao et al. report Master-RM, trained with a small share of adversarial negatives, has near-0% false positives across all tested attacks.
claim_before_audit: Search against a learned evaluator has an exploitable blind-spot class: optimized 100-token suffixes lift PRM reward above 0.9 on flawed reasoning, 43% of RL reward gain is style, and judge false positives reach 35-90% under master keys; patching one family fixed that family only.

claim: AlphaZero-style LLM tree search declines at the largest budget on GSM8K (53.6%, below ReSCALE 58.4% and just above Best-of-N 53.4%), and in an SC-MCTS* ablation on Blocksworld (step 6, hard mode) tuning the UCT constant away from the commonly used default of 1 added 5.27 points.
agent_test: Do not scale tree budget blindly; plot accuracy against budget on a held-out set.
audit_note: ReSCALE numbers (53.6/58.4/53.4) are exact, but SC-MCTS* only says the default C=1 led to 'potential failures'; the +5.27 is one ablation step (pseudo-random-reward base, Blocksworld step 6 hard mode), not evidence that default C=1 'failed'; 'decide whether more budget helps' is broader than either paper.
claim_before_audit: Root-selection and parameter choices decide whether more budget helps: AlphaZero-style LLM tree search declines at the largest budget (53.6% vs ReSCALE 58.4%, Best-of-N 53.4% on GSM8K), and default UCT C=1 failed on Blocksworld until tuned (+5.27 points).

claim: Depth helps or hurts depending on the model: on DeepMath level 9 at equal tokens, MCTS-style depth lifted instruct/RLVR models (+0.5% to +39%) and hurt base models (-10% to -29%); no clean MCTS vs sampling test on frontier reasoning models was found.
agent_test: Probe our model's diversity before choosing depth versus breadth.

claim: Early wrong steps are costly and weakly recovered in long-CoT models: forced wrong first step lowers accuracy from 94.8 to 28.5 (R1-Distill-7B) and from 100 to 78.7 (Qwen3-235B), so first-step checks are where verification pays; natural trap density is unmeasured.
agent_test: Add a code check on the first committed step.

claim: Noise in a step scorer makes deeper search riskier: bad prefixes get spuriously high scores more often as depth and candidates grow (theory, 14 of 16 settings better with a diversity-keeping selector); a depth cap should be tied to scorer noise.
agent_test: Keep two or more branches at each step rather than pruning to the top score.
